title: Neolithic Zagros and Proto-Elamite Susa
subtitle: 8,000–3,200 BC · From the First Farmers to the Dawn of Writing

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: From the first herding camps to the proto-urban centre and the dawn of writing at Susa

entries.label: Ganj Dareh and the First Herders
entries.hint: Excavations at Ganj Dareh in the central Zagros uncovered some of the earliest secure evidence anywhere for goat domestication, alongside plastered clay human and animal figurines and mudbrick houses — a settled community managing herds rather than only hunting them, among the very first anywhere in the world.
entries.note: Philip Smith, Ganj Dareh Tepe excavations (1967–74 seasons).

entries.label: Ali Kosh and Chogha Bonut — the First Farming Villages of Khuzestan
entries.hint: On the lowland plain below the Zagros, the villages of Ali Kosh and Chogha Bonut combined domesticated emmer wheat and barley with sheep and goat herding — evidence that farming reached the hot Khuzestan lowlands, the future heartland of Elam, from the highland Zagros rather than developing there independently.
entries.note: Frank Hole, Kent Flannery and James Neely, Prehistory and Human Ecology of the Deh Luran Plain (1969); Chogha Bonut excavations, Abbas Alizadeh (1996–97).

entries.label: Chogha Mish — the Rise of a Proto-Urban Centre
entries.hint: Chogha Mish grew across three millennia from a farming village into one of the largest and longest-occupied settlements in prehistoric Khuzestan, its later levels yielding stamp seals, clay counting tokens and a substantial administrative building — an urban trajectory that Susa would soon overtake and eclipse.
entries.note: Pinhas Delougaz and Helene Kantor, Chogha Mish: The First Five Seasons of Excavations, 1961–1971 (1996).

entries.label: The Founding of Susa
entries.hint: Susa was founded with a massive artificial terrace supporting a monumental platform, built at a scale far beyond ordinary village construction from its very first occupation — a planned religious and administrative centre from the outset rather than a settlement that grew into one.
entries.note: Roman Ghirshman and later Alain Le Brun, Susa excavations, on the Susa I 'Acropole' terrace.

entries.label: Susa II and Contact with Uruk
entries.hint: Susa's material culture shifted markedly toward styles shared with the expanding Mesopotamian city of Uruk — beveled-rim bowls, cylinder seals and administrative practices — evidence of Susa's incorporation into a wider southern Mesopotamian economic and cultural sphere well before it developed a fully independent identity.
entries.note: Guillermo Algaze, The Uruk World System (1993), on Susa's place in the Uruk expansion.

entries.label: The Proto-Elamite Script
entries.hint: Susa produced one of the world's earliest independent writing systems, proto-Elamite, on clay tablets recording economic transactions — a script that spread across the Iranian plateau as far as Tepe Sialk and Tepe Yahya but remains, unlike its Mesopotamian cuneiform contemporary, still undeciphered today.
entries.note: Proto-Elamite tablet corpus, Louvre and National Museum of Iran; Jacob Dahl, on the ongoing decipherment problem.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Evidence of violence and disruption across four prehistoric millennia

entries.label: Skeletal Trauma at Zagros Sites
entries.hint: Osteological analysis of burials from several Zagros Neolithic sites has identified a small but consistent proportion of healed and unhealed skeletal trauma consistent with interpersonal violence — evidence that even small, largely egalitarian farming communities were not free of conflict, though its scale and cause cannot be reconstructed in detail.
entries.note: Comparative bioarchaeological trauma studies of Zagros Neolithic skeletal populations.

entries.label: Abandonment at Ali Kosh
entries.hint: Ali Kosh was abandoned after roughly a millennium and a half of continuous occupation, for reasons excavators could not establish with certainty from the material evidence alone — a reminder that even a long-successful early farming settlement's ending is not always legible in the archaeological record the way its founding is.
entries.note: Frank Hole, Kent Flannery and James Neely, Prehistory and Human Ecology of the Deh Luran Plain (1969).

entries.label: The End of the Uruk Presence at Susa
entries.hint: The intensive Uruk-style material culture at Susa declined sharply toward the end of this period, coinciding with the wider collapse of the Uruk expansion's network across the region — whether through local resistance, economic disruption or a negotiated withdrawal remains debated among specialists.
entries.note: Guillermo Algaze, The Uruk World System (1993), on the Uruk network's collapse.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The first tokens of accounting and the earliest administrative seals

entries.label: Centralised Storage at Susa's Platform
entries.hint: Large storage vessels and evidence of controlled redistribution around Susa's monumental terrace point to an emerging authority managing agricultural surplus on behalf of the community from the settlement's earliest phase — a governing function exercised well before any king or named institution can be identified.
entries.note: Alain Le Brun, Susa excavations, on the Acropole terrace's storage and administrative function.

entries.label: Stamp Seals and the Control of Sealed Goods
entries.hint: Carved stamp seals impressed into clay sealings on storage jars and doors at Chogha Mish and Susa provided a physical means of marking goods as controlled or restricted property — a durable administrative technology of ownership and access control that long predates any written record of who held that authority.
entries.note: Pinhas Delougaz and Helene Kantor, Chogha Mish excavation reports, on the sealing corpus.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Plastered figurines, burial practice, and the temple platform at Susa

entries.label: Plastered Figurines at Ganj Dareh
entries.hint: Unbaked clay figurines of humans and animals from Ganj Dareh, some deliberately broken, are usually interpreted as ritual or fertility objects rather than toys or art for its own sake, though their precise function cannot be recovered from the archaeological evidence alone.
entries.note: Philip Smith, Ganj Dareh Tepe excavations, on the figurine assemblage.

entries.label: Zagros Neolithic Burial Practice
entries.hint: Intentional burials with grave goods — beads, tools, occasional painted vessels — at Ali Kosh and related sites show a consistent, if modest, mortuary practice treating the dead as deserving deliberate ritual attention rather than simple disposal.
entries.note: Frank Hole, Kent Flannery and James Neely, Prehistory and Human Ecology of the Deh Luran Plain (1969).

entries.label: The Susa I Cemetery
entries.hint: More than two thousand burials were recovered from beneath and around Susa's founding terrace, most accompanied by the site's famous painted beakers as funerary offerings — a mortuary program on a scale suggesting the terrace functioned as a communal cemetery and ritual centre from its very first generation of use.
entries.note: Roman Ghirshman, Susa excavations (1946–67 seasons), on the Susa I necropolis.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Painted pottery traditions of the Zagros and Khuzestan

entries.label: The Susiana Painted Pottery Tradition
entries.hint: A long sequence of painted pottery styles at Chogha Mish and related Khuzestan sites — geometric bands giving way to increasingly stylised animal and bird motifs — established a regional artistic vocabulary that the famous Susa I ware would inherit and refine rather than invent from nothing.
entries.note: Pinhas Delougaz and Helene Kantor, Chogha Mish excavation reports, on the Susiana ceramic sequence.

entries.label: The Susa I Painted Beakers
entries.hint: Tall, thin-walled buff pottery beakers painted with schematic ibex, long-necked birds and geometric bands, placed by the hundreds in Susa's founding cemetery, are among the most technically accomplished and widely reproduced images of Iranian prehistoric art — functional funerary vessels that were also, unmistakably, deliberate artistic statements.
entries.note: Susa I painted beaker corpus, Louvre Museum and National Museum of Iran.

entries.label: Susa's Monumental Terrace
entries.hint: Susa's founders raised an artificial platform of massive scale before any ordinary domestic architecture is attested at the site — a purpose-built ceremonial and administrative foundation whose ambition at the very start of occupation has no clear precedent among its Khuzestan predecessors.
entries.note: Alain Le Brun, Susa excavations, on the Acropole terrace's construction sequence.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Counting tokens, stamp seals, and the invention of proto-Elamite script

entries.label: Clay Tokens and the Origins of Counting
entries.hint: Small geometric clay tokens — cones, spheres, discs each representing a specific quantity of a specific commodity — appear at Khuzestan sites across millennia before writing, providing what many specialists regard as the direct conceptual ancestor of both proto-Elamite and cuneiform numerical notation.
entries.note: Denise Schmandt-Besserat, Before Writing: From Counting to Cuneiform (1992), on the token-to-script hypothesis.

entries.label: Cylinder Seals Introduced at Susa
entries.hint: Susa adopted the cylinder seal — a carved stone roller producing a continuous repeating image when rolled across wet clay — from the Uruk sphere during its period of closest Mesopotamian contact, a more versatile administrative and authenticating technology than the stamp seals it partly displaced.
entries.note: Susa cylinder seal corpus, Louvre Museum; Pierre Amiet, Glyptique susienne (1972).

entries.label: The Proto-Elamite Numerical System
entries.hint: Even though the proto-Elamite script's underlying language remains undeciphered, its numerical notation system — using distinct sign sets for counting different categories of goods such as grain, animals and human labour — has been successfully reconstructed, evidence of a sophisticated accounting logic operating independently of Mesopotamian cuneiform's own numerical conventions.
entries.note: Jacob Dahl, on the proto-Elamite numerical sign systems.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The domestication of goat and sheep, and the first farmed grain

entries.label: Goat and Sheep Domestication
entries.hint: Bone assemblages at Ganj Dareh showing a managed age-and-sex kill profile — young males culled while breeding females were kept — provide some of the clearest early evidence anywhere for deliberate goat herd management, a fundamental economic shift from hunting toward control over animal reproduction itself.
entries.note: Philip Smith, Ganj Dareh Tepe excavations, on the faunal kill-profile evidence.

entries.label: Emmer Wheat and Barley in Khuzestan
entries.hint: Carbonised grain remains at Ali Kosh show domesticated emmer wheat and two-row barley cultivated alongside herded sheep and goat — a mixed farming economy that let the Khuzestan lowlands support denser, more permanent settlement than the surrounding steppe.
entries.note: Frank Hole, Kent Flannery and James Neely, Prehistory and Human Ecology of the Deh Luran Plain (1969).

entries.label: Agricultural Surplus and Susa's Growth
entries.hint: Susa's rapid growth into a major centre rested on the agricultural productivity of the surrounding Khuzestan plain, whose surplus grain supported specialist craftspeople, administrators and the labour needed to raise the site's monumental terrace — population and political concentration built directly on an agrarian base.
entries.note: Robert McC. Adams, on the settlement-pattern evidence for Susiana plain agricultural intensification.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Pottery, irrigation, and the potter's wheel

entries.label: The Spread of Fired Pottery
entries.hint: Fired ceramic vessels replaced earlier basketry and unfired clay containers across Khuzestan sites during this period, a technology requiring controlled high-temperature kilns that also, incidentally, created the durable painted-pottery record archaeologists now use to trace cultural sequences across the whole region.
entries.note: Pinhas Delougaz and Helene Kantor, Chogha Mish excavation reports, on the ceramic technology sequence.

entries.label: Early Irrigation in Khuzestan
entries.hint: Settlement-pattern surveys of the Susiana plain show village distribution closely tracking artificial as well as natural watercourses by this period, evidence that simple irrigation channels were already extending cultivable land beyond the Karkheh river's immediate floodplain before Susa's rise to prominence.
entries.note: Robert McC. Adams, settlement-survey evidence for the Susiana plain irrigation network.

entries.label: The Slow Wheel and Mass-Produced Bowls
entries.hint: A slow-turning wheel (tournette) introduced during Susa's period of Uruk contact allowed the rapid, standardised mass production of simple beveled-rim bowls — probably used for distributing standard grain rations — a production-technology shift that also reflects a new scale of centralised labour organisation.
entries.note: Guillermo Algaze, The Uruk World System (1993), on beveled-rim bowl production and distribution.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Obsidian, shell and the Uruk network reaching Susa

entries.label: Anatolian Obsidian and Gulf Shell
entries.hint: Obsidian tools at Zagros and Khuzestan sites can be sourced by trace-element analysis to volcanic outcrops in eastern Anatolia hundreds of kilometres away, while marine shell ornaments at the same sites originated on the Persian Gulf coast — evidence of long-distance exchange networks operating millennia before any city or state existed to organise them.
entries.note: Trace-element sourcing studies of Zagros and Khuzestan obsidian assemblages.

entries.label: Uruk Settlers or Traders at Susa
entries.hint: The thoroughness of Uruk-style material culture at Susa during this period — not just imported objects but locally made Uruk-style pottery, architecture and administrative tools — has led some archaeologists to argue for actual Mesopotamian colonists resident at the site, rather than purely indirect trade contact, though the question remains actively debated.
entries.note: Guillermo Algaze, The Uruk World System (1993), on the colonisation-versus-contact debate for Susa.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: Climate, settlement growth, and the Uruk expansion's edge

entries.label: Holocene Warming and the Farming Transition
entries.hint: The warmer, wetter climate of the early Holocene, following the end of the last glacial period, created the ecological conditions across the Zagros and its foothills that made systematic plant cultivation and animal herding a viable, and eventually dominant, way of life for the first time.
entries.note: Paleoclimate proxy evidence for the Younger Dryas-to-Holocene transition in the Zagros region.

entries.label: The Uruk Expansion's Eastern Edge
entries.hint: Susa marked the easternmost significant node of the Uruk expansion's network of trade colonies and cultural influence radiating from southern Mesopotamia — placing Khuzestan, and Susa specifically, within a genuinely interregional system centuries before any textual record could describe the relationship in its own words.
entries.note: Guillermo Algaze, The Uruk World System (1993).

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Diet, health and the archaeology of daily life

entries.group: Health and Diet in the Farming Transition
entries.label: Skeletal Evidence of Dietary Change
entries.hint: Dental wear and pathology patterns in skeletal remains from early farming villages show measurable changes from earlier hunter-gatherer populations — increased caries and altered wear consistent with a diet now centred on cultivated grain — physical, bodily evidence of a transition usually described only in economic terms.
entries.note: Comparative bioarchaeological dental studies of Zagros and Khuzestan Neolithic populations.

entries.label: Emerging Social Differentiation at Susa
entries.hint: Grave goods in the Susa I cemetery vary noticeably in quantity and quality between burials, evidence that meaningful social and economic differentiation between individuals or families had emerged alongside the settlement's rapid growth — the archaeological signature of inequality appearing as a new social category, not yet expressed in any surviving text.
entries.note: Roman Ghirshman, Susa excavations, on grave-good variability in the Susa I necropolis.
